EthSwitch, Ethiopia's national payment switch operator, achieved PCI DSS v3.2.1 certification in 2020 following third-party security audits conducted by SISA Information Security across its issuing, acquiring and authorisation services; EthSwitch's own System Rules (2025) further confirm it has audit powers over participants. This is evidence of an external audit having occurred and being publicly announced, but the detailed audit findings/report are not themselves published, so this best fits 'Private Audits' rather than 'Public Audits'. Score raised from 0 (Unknown) to 2 (Private Audits). No audit evidence specific to Telebirr was found. Because the only concrete audit evidence dates to 2020 and it is unclear whether this reflects an ongoing/regular audit regime, flagging for human review to confirm currency.
revised_comments: EthSwitch, Ethiopia's national payment switch operator, has undergone third-party security audits, achieving PCI DSS v3.2.1 certification from SISA Information Security in 2020 covering its issuing, acquiring and authorisation services. EthSwitch's System Rules give it authority to audit participant institutions, but the detailed findings of external audits of EthSwitch itself are not published; only the fact of certification is publicly disclosed. No specific evidence of independent audits of Telebirr was identified.

Definition: Whether digital payment systems and access points (apps, USSD, agents) are designed to accommodate persons with disabilities (visual, hearing, mobility, cognitive impairments), and disability-disaggregated coverage rates if data available.
Comments: No evidence for disability access in payment systems.
redteam_note: Scored 0/Unknown with no source — confirm it is truly unknown, not just unresearched. No data year recorded — provenance/recency unknown.
revision_notes: Light Exa check surfaced authoritative evidence, so this row was moved from the fast path to the full path. Ethio Telecom's Telebirr mobile money platform (2025) offers IVR, USSD and app-based access with voice-command functionality for visually impaired users, plus discounted connectivity packages for persons with disabilities, and Bank of Abyssinia has piloted talking ATMs. However, a 2025-26 sector analysis (DFS Ethiopia Hub) notes Ethiopia's National Financial Inclusion Strategy (NFIS II) sets no binding accessibility standards, and most banking apps/ATMs still lack screen-reader support. Score raised from 0 (Unknown) to 2 (Partial), reflecting real but uneven accommodation concentrated in one major provider rather than sector-wide.
revised_comments: Ethiopia's dominant mobile money platform, Telebirr (operated by Ethio Telecom), provides accessibility features including IVR, USSD and app-based access with voice-command functionality for people with visual impairments, alongside discounted connectivity packages of up to 35% for persons with disabilities. Ethio Telecom has partnered with disability organisations, including the Ethiopian Center for Disability and Development, to develop accessible information services and has funded assistive devices. Some banks, including the Bank of Abyssinia, have piloted voice-assisted talking ATMs. Ethiopia's National Financial Inclusion Strategy does not mandate binding accessibility standards, however, and most banking apps and ATMs still lack comprehensive screen-reader support or physical accessibility features, so accommodation for persons with disabilities remains partial rather than systemic across the sector.

revision_notes: Light Exa check surfaced partial evidence, so this row was moved from the fast path to the full path. The National Bank of Ethiopia's own draft NDPS 2.0 strategy (published December 2025) lists 'government payment systems remain fragmented' as a current sector gap, but gives no economy-wide percentage. World Bank reporting indicates around 1.5 million of roughly 9 million Productive Safety Net Programme households (about 17%) received electronic transfers as of December 2022, but this covers only one social-transfer programme, not the full G2P envelope (salaries, pensions, all social transfers) the variable requires. No comprehensive percentage figure for total government digital payment adoption was found. Evidence points toward a low percentage but is not precise enough to confidently assign a scale band, so the code is left unchanged at 0 (Unknown) and flagged for human review rather than asserted.
revised_comments: Ethiopia's National Bank identifies fragmented government payment systems as a continuing challenge in its 2026-2030 digital payments strategy (BRIDGE 2030). Some government social transfer programmes have moved to electronic disbursement: as of December 2022 around 1.5 million of roughly 9 million Productive Safety Net Programme beneficiary households received payments electronically via bank accounts, though comprehensive published data on the overall share of government salaries, pensions and social transfers made digitally is not available.

Definition: Whether refugees, asylum seekers, internally displaced persons, migrants, and stateless persons can legally access and open digital payment accounts, and practical barriers or enablers for these populations.
Comments: No evidence for refugee/migrant specific digital payment access.
redteam_note: Scored 0/Unknown with no source — confirm it is truly unknown, not just unresearched. No data year recorded — provenance/recency unknown.
revision_notes: Light Exa check surfaced strong authoritative evidence, so this row was moved from the fast path to the full path. Ethiopia's Refugee Proclamation No. 1110/2019 grants refugees legal access to banking and telecom services, and since 2023 refugees have been progressively enrolled in the national Fayda digital ID system, which is explicitly recognised by banks and mobile network operators for account opening, SIM registration and TIN issuance. This is corroborated by a UNHCR report (September 2025) and a World Bank project appraisal document for the Digital ID for Inclusion and Services Project (2024-2029), which is funding refugee registration specifically. Score raised from 0 (Unknown) to 3 (Yes), reflecting both legal entitlement and practical enablement via the digital ID system.
revised_comments: Ethiopia's Refugee Proclamation No. 1110/2019 grants refugees and asylum-seekers legal rights to access banking and telecommunications services. Since 2023, refugees have been progressively enrolled in the national Fayda digital ID system (National ID Programme), which issues them a verifiable digital identification number recognised by banks, mobile network operators and other service providers. With a Fayda-enabled refugee ID, refugees can open bank accounts, register SIM cards, obtain a Tax Identification Number and access microfinance, removing the need for case-by-case endorsement letters previously required from the Refugees and Returnees Service. The World Bank-supported Digital ID for Inclusion and Services Project (2024-2029) is funding continued registration and issuance of Fayda credentials to refugee populations, including in host communities such as Benishangul-Gumuz.
